report.verdict: Lithuania's regulated gambling market is compounding at mid-teens rates — 9M-26 GGR €229m (~$250.5m), +14% — almost entirely on online slots, with remote now 78% of GGR and retail shrinking 6.5%. But the state is about to take a much larger cut and a much tighter grip: a 22%→36% progressive GGR tax proposed from July 2027, a full advertising ban from January 2028 and a mandatory player card with cashless venues from 2029. The commercial window is real but narrowing, and it belongs to scale incumbents; for a newcomer the only credible routes are acquisition of a licensee or B2B supply.
summary: **Market is €229m (~$250.5m) of gambling GGR in 9M-26, +14% YoY** (9M-25: €200.5m / ~$219.3m), on top of FY25 GGR €274.1m (~$299.9m, +13%), FY24 €241.9m (~$264.6m, +8.85%) and FY23 €222.2m (~$243.1m). Growth is accelerating, not fading — all figures are regulator (LPT) GGR = stakes minus winnings, before tax, excluding lotteries.

**Online is the market: remote GGR €179.0m (~$195.8m), +21.8%, 78% of total** (73% in 9M-25, 74% FY25, 70% FY24; remote overtook retail in 2020). H1-26 remote was €119.9m (~$131.2m, +24.8%); derived Q3-26 remote €59.1m (~$64.7m, +~16%) shows some deceleration from H1.

**One product carries everything: remote Category A slots €131.6m (~$144.0m), +~30% (+€30.4m), 57% of all gambling GGR.** The slots gain alone exceeded the whole market's net increase (+€28.5m), i.e. every other category combined shrank by ~€1.9m. Online slots+tables+Cat B = €149.9m (~$164.0m), 65% of market GGR.

**Betting is stalling despite a World Cup summer: remote betting GGR €29.1m (~$31.8m), −2%; retail betting €4.9m (~$5.4m), down.** Combined betting is only ~15% of GGR. The 2026 FIFA World Cup (Jun–Jul) sat inside the period and still did not lift the line; LPT does not publish handle, so hold cannot be isolated (n/a).

**Online table games €17.7m (~$19.4m), +24%** (H1 +34%, so Q3 slowed to ~+6% derived); remote Category B machines collapsed −67% to €0.6m (~$0.7m) as play migrates to Cat A; online bingo is dead (€284).

**Retail is in structural decline: land-based GGR €50.0m (~$54.7m), −6.5%** (H1 −5%, derived Q3 −~10%). Split: Cat B slot halls €22.2m (~$24.3m), casino Cat A machines €12.1m (~$13.2m, slightly up), tables €10.8m (~$11.8m, down), betting shops €4.9m. Machines in venues fell to 3,736 from 3,914 (−4.5%).

**Lottery is a separate, resilient duopoly: ticket sales €131.5m (~$143.9m), +9%; prizes €74.2m (~$81.2m, 56% payout); lottery GGR €57.3m (~$62.7m).** FY25 sales were €167.2m (~$182.9m, +12.7%) with prizes €91.9m (~$100.5m). Two private operators as of 30 Jun 2026. Adding lottery GGR, the combined 9M-26 market is ~€286m (~$313m).

**Fiscal take €74.19m (~$81.2m), +15%**: gambling operators ~€50m (~$54.7m), lottery operators €24.2m (~$26.5m). FY25 take was €86.9m (~$95.1m; gambling €57.6m, lottery €29.3m), FY24 €73.9m (~$80.9m). Gambling tax ÷ GGR = 21.8%, which independently corroborates the 22% headline rate; lottery tax ÷ sales = 18.4%, corroborating 18% on turnover.

**Tax regime (Lottery and Gaming Tax Law, VMI): 22% of GGR** on slots, table games, bingo, totalisator, betting and remote gambling since 1 Jan 2025 (20% from 1 Jul 2022), **plus a fixed monthly amount per licensed retail device**; **lotteries 18% of the nominal value of tickets sold (turnover base)** since 1 Jan 2023; quarterly tax periods; one-off licence-issuance fee. No player-level withholding at operator level.

**Tax cliff ahead: the Finance Ministry published amendments on ~10 Nov 2026** raising lottery tax 18%→20% and making gambling tax progressive — 22% on GGR up to €3m (~$3.3m), 29% on €3–5m, 36% above €5m (~$5.5m) — targeted for 1 Jul 2027 (per Casino Guardian/iGamingToday). The sponsor (Democrats' T. Tomilinas) cites +€36m (~$39m) p.a. With all eight operators well above €5m GGR, the effective market rate is ~35%, not 22%.

**Politics are one-directional.** A rival LVŽS bill (lottery 25%, gambling 30%, licence fee doubled to €2m/~$2.2m) received a negative Government opinion in Sept 2026, and the Ministry had resisted a 22–37% progressive bill in 2025 — yet within months the Ministry tabled its own progressive scale to fund the 2027 budget. Every coalition partner is now on record for higher gambling taxes; only the scale is in play.

**Licensing is closed in practice.** LPT (Lošimų priežiūros tarnyba, under the Ministry of Finance) licenses by game type under the Gaming Law IX-325 (2001; remote since 2016). LPT counts 12 licensed gambling companies, of which 8 operate (unchanged YoY; 12 operated in 2022, 12 of 15 licensed in 2020). Remote licences have historically been tied to holding a domestic land-based licence [per the 2016 regime; current text not re-verified].

**Operator landscape is an oligopoly with no per-operator disclosure.** The four-member Responsible Gambling Business Association says it represents ~60% of the 2024 market. Active brands include TOPsport, Betsafe (Betsson), Olybet, 7bet, Uniclub, Cbet and Optibet [brand list from market knowledge, not from the LPT register in this research]; market shares n/a.

**Player-protection overhaul (Draft Law XVP-1690):** submitted 2 Apr 2026, approved by Government in June 2026, notified to the EU TRIS system 18 Aug 2026, Seimas adoption pending. Expanded LPT powers and streamlined compliance from 1 May 2027; a mandatory, ID-linked player card for retail and online plus cashless venues from 1 Jan 2029; affordability checks for higher-spending players. Separately, Law XV-517 (13 Nov 2025) gives the self-exclusion register its own article with a 6-month minimum from 1 Jan 2027.

**Advertising is being switched off.** The Gaming Law already prohibits gambling advertising and promotion (including incentive bonuses) with narrow exceptions; from 1 Jul 2025 outdoor advertising is limited to name/trademark; a complete ban applies from 1 Jan 2028 (per multiple secondary sources). Licensed operators cannot buy market share — a decisive structural advantage for incumbents.

**Payments are euro, bank-centric and about to go cashless in venues** (from 2029, tied to the player card, with a 3-year equipment transition). Detailed online payment-method data is not published (n/a).

**Enforcement is active but uneven:** in 2025 LPT issued 47 warnings to foreign entities and ran 37 illegal-remote investigations; it blocked Polymarket in Sept 2026 as unlicensed betting while Kalshi stayed accessible (LRT, Oct 2026). Licensed operators complained to LPT in Feb 2026 about unlicensed brands advertising in Lithuania. Illegal-market size: n/a.

**Quarterly cadence:** Gaming Intelligence reports Q1-26 €82.7m (~$90.5m, +4%) and a record Q2-26 €109.3m (~$119.6m, +24%); these appear to include lottery GGR (Q1+Q2 = €192.0m ≈ gambling GGR €153.6m + ~€38m lottery GGR). Gambling-only Q3-26 derived from LPT data is €75.4m (~$82.5m), +~9% — the slowest quarter of the year.

**Read-through for B2Tech:** a small (~2.9m people), fast-growing, online-led, high-margin market that is about to become high-tax (~35% effective), ad-dark and card-gated. Greenfield entry is impractical; value lies in (i) acquiring a licensee before the 2027 tax reset is priced in, (ii) supplying slots/live content, platform and compliance/payment tech to the eight incumbents, and (iii) retail consolidation as cashless capex forces marginal halls out.

segments.name: Online casino (remote Category A/B slots and table games)
segments.headline: Online slots are the Lithuanian market: €131.6m (~$144.0m) 9M-26 GGR, +~30%, 57% of all gambling GGR — and the only category that is growing the pie.
narrative: LPT's 9M-26 release puts remote Category A machine (slot) GGR at €131.6m (~$144.0m), up roughly a third on 9M-25 (€101.2m derived) and equal to 57% of total gambling GGR and ~74% of remote GGR. H1-26 was €85.7m (~$93.8m, +~33%), which implies a derived Q3-26 of €45.9m (~$50.2m), still +~25% YoY. The +€30.4m YoY gain exceeded the whole market's +€28.5m, so ex-slots the regulated market contracted by ~€1.9m. This is the single most important fact in the market: growth is a slots story, and every policy lever now being pulled (progressive tax, affordability checks, player-card limits) lands squarely on this category.

Remote table games (including live dealer) reached €17.7m (~$19.4m), +24% YoY (9M-25 ≈ €14.3m). The H1 print was €12.3m (~$13.5m, +34%), so the derived Q3 figure of ~€5.4m (~$5.9m) grew only ~6% — the first visible deceleration in the online casino complex. Remote Category B machines fell 67% to €0.61m (~$0.67m) as operators migrate content to the Cat A category, and online bingo recorded €284 for the period — commercially extinct.

Taken together, online casino (Cat A + Cat B + tables) generated ~€149.9m (~$164.0m) in 9M-26, about 65% of gambling GGR and 84% of remote GGR. On a simple run-rate the vertical is tracking toward ~€200m (~$219m) for FY26 (estimate). Notably this growth is being achieved with no permitted bonuses or incentive promotions and with outdoor advertising restricted since 1 Jul 2025 — i.e. it is organic/product-led and partly a channel shift from retail slot halls (whose GGR fell) and, plausibly, from offshore sites following LPT blocking and warnings.

The regulator does not publish active accounts, deposits or RTP by operator, so ARPU and player-count trends are n/a; the association of four large licensees claims ~60% of the 2024 market, which implies the top two or three online operators dominate slots. For a supplier, demand is for slots content, aggregation and live tables delivered into eight licensed platforms; for an operator, the forward risk is the 36% top tax band (effective ~35% on a scale casino book) and the 2029 card-linked limits, which Scandinavian precedents suggest can knock double-digit percentages off regulated casino GGR.

segments.name: Sports betting (remote and retail)
segments.headline: Betting is a ~15% side-vertical that went backwards (−2% online) through a World Cup summer; LPT publishes no handle, so hold is n/a.
narrative: Remote betting GGR was €29.1m (~$31.8m) in 9M-26, down 2% on a derived 9M-25 base of ~€29.7m; betting-shop GGR was €4.9m (~$5.4m), also down (prior-year retail figure not disclosed). Combined betting of ~€34.0m (~$37.2m) is 14.8% of gambling GGR and 16% of remote GGR. LPT's statistical release reports GGR only — stakes, hold, promo intensity and structural margin are not disclosed (n/a), so it is impossible to say from primary data whether the decline is results-driven or volume-driven.

The 2026 FIFA World Cup (June–July) fell inside Q2/Q3, which makes a flat-to-down betting print unusually weak for a market growing 14% overall. Plausible contributors are the ban on incentive promotions (no free bets to drive event acquisition), operators' pricing in a 22% GGR tax environment, and leakage to unlicensed sportsbooks and prediction markets. On that last point LPT ordered Polymarket blocked in September 2026 on the basis that its product is unlicensed betting, while Kalshi remained accessible — an inconsistency criticised publicly by MP M. Lingė (LRT, Oct 2026).

Retail betting infrastructure is thin and shrinking: LPT's 2020 annual report counted 131 betting points among 349 gambling venues at end-2020; a current count was not retrievable (n/a), but the €4.9m retail betting GGR is under 10% of land-based GGR. Betting is thus overwhelmingly a digital product bundled with casino, and the economics of a sportsbook-led entry are poor.

For an operator the forward issue is the tax base: at an assumed ~8% hold, a 36% top GGR rate equals ~3% of handle, which is heavy for a product that must compete on price with offshore books. Expect incumbents to treat betting as a cross-sell funnel into slots rather than a profit centre, and expect the progressive tax, if adopted, to widen pricing gaps versus unlicensed operators further.

segments.name: Land-based venues (casinos, slot halls, betting shops)
segments.headline: Retail GGR €50.0m (~$54.7m), −6.5% and accelerating downward (derived Q3 −~10%); 3,736 machines and a 2029 cashless mandate point to managed decline and consolidation.
narrative: Land-based GGR fell to €50.0m (~$54.7m) in 9M-26 from €53.5m (~$58.5m), with LPT noting lower stakes, prizes and revenue across the board. H1-26 was €33.7m (~$36.9m, −5%), so the derived Q3-26 figure of €16.3m (~$17.8m) was down ~10% YoY — the rate of decline is increasing. Retail's share of gambling GGR is now 22%, versus 30% in FY24 and parity as recently as 2019–20.

By product, Category B machines in slot halls remain the largest retail line at €22.2m (~$24.3m), followed by casino Category A machines at €12.1m (~$13.2m, slightly up), table games €10.8m (~$11.8m, down; H1 €7.7m was flat, implying a weak Q3 of ~€3.1m) and betting shops €4.9m (~$5.4m). The installed base of gaming machines fell to 3,736 at end-September 2026 from 3,914 a year earlier (−4.5%). For context, LPT's 2020 annual report listed 17 casinos, 201 slot halls and 131 betting points; SBC News (May 2026) cited LPT figures of 18 casinos, 50 'arcade halls' and 10 online licences, which is inconsistent with earlier counts and is flagged as unverified.

Retail carries a dual tax burden — 22% of GGR plus a fixed monthly amount per licensed machine/table, payable quarterly — and faces the heaviest capex from the reform package: from 1 Jan 2029 all payments and payouts in venues must be non-cash and tied to the player card, with a three-year transition explicitly granted so operators can replace or upgrade equipment. Combined with the 2028 advertising ban, this will push marginal halls out; the fall in machine numbers is the leading indicator.

Commercially, land-based assets matter mainly as licence anchors and brand touchpoints: historically a Lithuanian remote licence has been available only to companies holding the corresponding land-based licence [2016 regime; current text not re-verified]. That makes small retail licensees potential acquisition vehicles for an online-led entrant, and makes 2027–29 the likely window for distressed consolidation.

segments.name: Lotteries
segments.headline: A two-operator segment with €131.5m (~$143.9m) of 9M-26 ticket sales (+9%) and €57.3m (~$62.7m) GGR, taxed at 18% of turnover (≈42% of GGR) and proposed to rise to 20%.
narrative: LPT reports lottery ticket sales of €131.5m (~$143.9m) for 9M-26, +9% YoY, with prizes of €74.2m (~$81.2m, +9.3%) — a 56.4% payout — leaving lottery operators €57.3m (~$62.7m) of gross revenue, up ~8.7% on a derived 9M-25 base of ~€52.8m. H1-26 sales were €87.73m (~$96.0m, +8.6%). FY25 sales were €167.2m (~$182.9m, +12.7% vs FY24 €148.3m) with prizes of €91.9m (~$100.5m), i.e. FY25 lottery GGR of ~€75.3m (~$82.4m). Lottery GGR is therefore roughly one-fifth of the combined gambling-plus-lottery market (~€286m in 9M-26).

Two private companies organised the large lotteries as of 30 June 2026 (LPT). Olifėja is the long-standing national operator (Eurojackpot, Vikinglotto, Teleloto); the identity and share of the second operator were not verified in this research, and LPT does not publish per-operator sales. The segment is effectively closed: licences are few, and the Lotteries Law also obliges operators to fund statutory support (parama) — LPT's 2020–22 overview shows €5.2–10.3m (~$5.7–11.3m) p.a. of such contributions.

Lottery tax is levied on turnover, not GGR: 18% of the nominal value of tickets sold since 1 Jan 2023 (13% from 1 Jul 2022; a lower rate before that). On the 9M-26 base that produced €24.2m (~$26.5m), 18.4% of sales and ~42% of lottery GGR. The Finance Ministry's November 2026 draft lifts the rate to 20% from July 2027, worth ~+€2.6m (~$2.9m) on the 9M-26 base and ~+€3.5m annualised; the rival LVŽS bill proposed 25%. Either way the lottery effective tax on GGR heads toward 45–55%, which is why operators have pushed back on payout economics.

For an operator the lottery segment is not an entry route, but it matters as a competitor for the same discretionary wallet and as a political benchmark: lawmakers repeatedly pair lottery and gambling tax rises in the same bills, so lottery-tax politics are a leading indicator for gambling-tax outcomes.

segments.name: Licensing & tax regime
segments.headline: A closed, game-type licence system under LPT with a 22% GGR tax (plus per-device charges) that is heading to a 22/29/36% progressive scale from July 2027 — an effective ~35% for every incumbent.
narrative: The framework rests on the Gaming Law (Azartinių lošimų įstatymas, No. IX-325, 2001), the Lotteries Law and the Lottery and Gaming Tax Law, supervised by the Gaming Control Authority (Lošimų priežiūros tarnyba, LPT) under the Ministry of Finance; remote gambling has been licensable domestically since 2016. Licences are issued per game type — table games and Category A machines (casinos), Category B machines (slot halls), bingo, totalisator, betting, and remote gambling — and a remote licence has historically required the corresponding land-based licence [2016 regime; not re-verified]. LPT lists 12 licensed gambling companies of which 8 operate (unchanged YoY), down from 12 operating in 2022 and 12 of 15 licensed in 2020; at end-2020 there were 7 remote betting, 5 remote table, 7 remote Cat A and 6 remote Cat B licensees. The minimum gambling age under the Gaming Law is 18 [not re-verified in this research].

Fees: the Lottery and Gaming Tax Law levies a one-off fee for the issuance of a gambling licence; press coverage of the LVŽS bill to 'double the price of the permit for all these games to €2m (~$2.2m)' implies the current amount is ~€1m (~$1.1m) [statutory schedule not verified]. Minimum authorised-capital thresholds apply by licence type (amounts n/a). Local establishment is required; server-location and local-ownership rules were not verified here (n/a).

Tax (VMI): the base for machines, tables, bingo, totalisator, betting and remote gambling is GGR (stakes less winnings actually paid), taxed at 22% since 1 Jan 2025 (20% from 1 Jul 2022; the 2025 step was scored at ~+€4.4m/~$4.8m), plus a fixed monthly amount per gaming device listed on a venue permit; lotteries pay 18% of the nominal value of tickets sold; the tax period is the calendar quarter. Actual collections corroborate the schedule: gambling-operator tax of ~€50m on €229m GGR = 21.8%; lottery tax €24.2m on €131.5m sales = 18.4%. FY24 sector data also show €32.6m (~$35.7m) of other taxes and fees and 1,561 employees.

The pipeline is the story. (1) The Finance Ministry's draft (published ~10 Nov 2026): lottery 18%→20%; gambling 22% on GGR ≤€3m, 29% on €3–5m, 36% above €5m, targeted for 1 Jul 2027, sponsor estimate +€36m (~$39m) p.a. (2) The LVŽS (Girskienė) bill: lottery 25%, gambling 30%, licence fee €2m — negative Government opinion, Sept 2026, but still before the Seimas. (3) The Democrats' 2025 bill for 22–37% from April 2026, which the Ministry rejected at the time as premature given player-card investment needs. With every operating licensee far above €5m GGR, the progressive scale is a flat ~35% in practice (e.g. €60m GGR → €21.0m tax, 35.1%); at market level, gambling tax would rise from ~€67m (22% of a ~€305m FY26E base) to ~€105m. For a licensee running a 30% EBITDA margin at 22%, a 13-point rise removes ~40% of EBITDA before mitigation (RTP cuts, odds margin, cost take-out), and B2B revenue-share contracts will be renegotiated accordingly.

segments.name: Player protection, advertising, payments & enforcement
segments.headline: Lithuania is building an EU-first centralised control stack — mandatory ID-linked player card, cashless venues and affordability checks by 2029 — on top of an advertising regime that goes fully dark on 1 Jan 2028.
narrative: Draft Law XVP-1690 amending the Gaming Law was submitted by the Finance Ministry on 2 Apr 2026, approved by the Government in June 2026 and notified to the EU TRIS system on 18 Aug 2026; it still requires Seimas adoption. It would (i) make a personal player card — physical or digital, linked to the player's profile and national ID number and integrated with the self-exclusion register — mandatory for all land-based and remote gambling from 1 Jan 2029, phased in through 2027–28; (ii) require that from 1 Jan 2029 all venue payments and payouts are non-cash and card-linked, with a three-year equipment transition; (iii) introduce affordability checks for higher-spending players who select larger limits; and (iv) expand LPT's powers and streamline operator compliance from 1 May 2027. Finance Minister K. Vaitiekūnas and PM I. Ruginienė have backed the package; LPT describes the card as the core tool for enforcing pre-set limits. Separately, Law XV-517 of 13 Nov 2025 (amending Articles 9-1 and 15-3) gives the self-exclusion register its own article with a six-month minimum exclusion from 1 Jan 2027. LRT also reported (May 2026) a proposal for a €1,000 (~$1,094) per-month loss limit; its legislative status is unverified.

Advertising is already heavily constrained and is being eliminated. The Gaming Law prohibits gambling advertising and promotion, including incentives such as bonuses, subject to narrow exceptions; from 1 Jul 2025 outdoor advertising may show only an operator's name and trademark, and a complete advertising ban is scheduled for 1 Jan 2028 (per focusgn, iGamingToday, Casino Guardian). The Responsible Gambling Business Association (four licensees, ~60% of the 2024 market) wrote to LPT on 6 and 26 Feb 2026 complaining that foreign brands without Lithuanian rights were advertising in the country; LPT's reply (24 Feb 2026, No. 2E-272) took the view that such promotion falls under the prohibition. The practical effect is that customer acquisition in Lithuania is brand-, SEO- and product-led only; a newcomer cannot buy awareness.

Enforcement: LPT maintains a blacklist of illegal gambling sites updated by director orders (e.g. 24 Apr 2026) and blocks access through ISPs; in 2025 it issued 47 warnings to foreign entities and conducted 37 investigations into illegal remote gambling, delivered 2,160 consultations and ran AML/CTF training for licensees. In Sept 2026 it ordered Polymarket blocked as an unlicensed betting product, while Kalshi remained accessible — an inconsistency criticised in the Seimas. LPT's 2020–22 overview benchmarked the illegal share of the market against Latvia, but a current illegal-market estimate was not retrievable (n/a); a 15min report (Nov 2026) on tax lost to illegal gambling could not be read in full.

Payments: the market is euro-denominated and bank-rail based (bank transfers/cards; e-wallet and open-banking usage not published, n/a); cash remains legal in venues until the 2029 cashless mandate, after which every venue transaction will be identity-linked through the player card. For operators and suppliers this creates a 2027–29 demand wave for identity, limit-management and cashless-payment technology, and a corresponding compliance-cost burden that the Ministry itself cited in 2025 as a reason to delay tax rises — a reason it has since dropped.

highlights.text: Structural online growth with no sign of saturation: remote GGR +21.8% in 9M-26 (€179.0m / ~$195.8m) after +19% in FY25 and +14.9% in FY24; online casino alone is tracking to ~€200m (~$219m) for FY26 (estimate). Online penetration of 78% already matches Nordic benchmarks.

A protected oligopoly: 8 operating licensees, no bonus competition, advertising restricted — so incumbent margins are high and customer bases sticky. For an entrant that means acquiring a licensee buys a defensible position, and the 2027 tax reset may create motivated sellers before it is priced in.

Slots dominance (57% of GGR, +30%) is a direct B2B demand signal for content, aggregation and live-casino supply into eight platforms; growth is product-led because promotions are banned, which rewards suppliers with differentiated titles.

Retail consolidation window 2027–29: machine count already −4.5% YoY, retail GGR −6.5% and a cashless/player-card capex mandate by 1 Jan 2029 will force marginal slot halls and small licensees to exit — opportunities to acquire licences and footprint cheaply.

Fiscal and legal predictability relative to emerging markets: euro, EU member, GGR-based tax (not turnover for gambling), quarterly filing, published regulator statistics, and a regulator that actively blocks and warns offshore competitors (47 warnings, 37 investigations in 2025; Polymarket blocked).

The player-card/cashless mandate creates a 2027–29 procurement cycle for identity, limit-management, affordability and cashless-payment technology across all licensees — a niche for compliance-tech and platform suppliers.

Tax take is growing faster than the market (+15% vs +14% GGR) without yet denting growth — evidence that the regulated channel is still winning share from offshore, at least until the ad ban and card land.

lowlights.text: Tax cliff: the Finance Ministry's 22/29/36% progressive scale from 1 Jul 2027 is a flat ~35% for every incumbent (all are >€5m GGR), lifting gambling tax from ~€67m to ~€105m on a ~€305m base. A 30%-margin licensee loses ~40% of EBITDA before mitigation; B2B revenue-share contracts will be repriced.

Advertising goes fully dark on 1 Jan 2028 on top of an existing promotion/bonus ban — a newcomer cannot build brand, and affiliate/SEO channels will be the only acquisition route. This freezes market shares in favour of TOPsport/Betsafe-tier incumbents.

Mandatory ID-linked player card, affordability checks and cashless venues from 2029 will bite hardest on the slots category that is 57% of GGR; Scandinavian precedents (Norway's card, Sweden's limits) point to double-digit regulated-GGR losses and offshore leakage, and the Polymarket/Kalshi inconsistency shows enforcement is not airtight.

Betting is weak: remote betting GGR −2% through a World Cup summer and only ~15% of the market; LPT publishes no handle, so margin trends cannot be diagnosed. A sportsbook-led thesis does not work here.

Retail decline is accelerating (−5% H1, −~10% derived Q3) and carries a dual tax burden (22% GGR plus per-device charges) and a cashless capex bill — retail assets are liabilities except as licence anchors.

Small, concentrated market: ~2.9m people, €274m (~$300m) FY25 GGR, eight operators, two lottery companies and a single regulator whose powers expand from May 2027. Policy risk is binary and idiosyncratic.

Governance volatility: three competing tax bills in 18 months (Democrats 22–37%, LVŽS 30%/25% with a €2m licence fee, MoF 22/29/36%), with the Ministry reversing its 2025 'not yet' position to fund the 2027 budget — the direction is clear but the final rate, thresholds and timing are not.

Data gaps: LPT does not publish actives, deposits, handle or per-operator shares, and its portal was not directly retrievable in this research; licence-fee and venue-count figures cited in press are inconsistent and flagged unverified.

forecast.intro: The regulatory bridge runs from today's comparatively liberal settings — a flat 22% GGR tax, outdoor-only advertising limits and voluntary player limits — to a 2027–29 regime of a 22/29/36% progressive GGR tax (effective ~35%), lottery tax at 20%, a complete advertising ban (1 Jan 2028) and a mandatory ID-linked player card with cashless venues and affordability checks (1 Jan 2029). The driver is fiscal: the Finance Ministry needs 2027 budget revenue and its coalition partners (the Democrats 'Vardan Lietuvos' and LVŽS) have each tabled steeper variants; the player-protection track (Draft Law XVP-1690) was approved by Government in June 2026, cleared EU TRIS notification in August and awaits the Seimas. The moving parts are the thresholds (€3m/€5m), the start date (July 2027 vs earlier), whether the LVŽS €2m licence fee survives, and the affordability thresholds LPT will set in secondary legislation.

forecast.view: **Revenue:** we estimate FY26 gambling GGR of ~€310m (~$339m), +13% (9M actual €229m plus a Q4 of ~€82m assuming +12% on Q4-25's €73.6m), with online share ending the year at ~79%. **FY27E +6–9%** as the July 2027 tax step is partly passed through via lower RTP and wider betting margins, and **2028 flat to −3%** once advertising goes dark; **2029 −5–10%** is the realistic downside when the card and affordability checks arrive, with online share nonetheless rising to 83–85% as retail keeps shrinking ~8–10% a year. **Tax take:** combined collections of ~€100m (~$109m) in FY26E rising to ~€135–145m (~$148–159m) in 2028 if the progressive scale is adopted — the state's revenue grows even as operator EBITDA falls by roughly a third. **Margins:** incumbents will defend through RTP cuts, cost take-out and renegotiated supplier revenue shares; expect at least one or two of the eight operators to exit or merge, leaving 5–6 by 2029. **Leverage/illegal share:** offshore leakage rises with each step, and the Polymarket/Kalshi episode suggests enforcement will remain reactive. **Our stance:** attractive to supply, hazardous to enter greenfield; any acquisition must be underwritten at a 36% top rate and zero advertising.
watch: Seimas handling of the Lottery and Gaming Tax Law amendments within the 2027 budget cycle (Dec 2026–spring 2027): final rates, the €3m/€5m thresholds, the July 2027 start date and whether the LVŽS €2m licence-fee rider is attached.
Seimas adoption and any EU TRIS comments on Draft Law XVP-1690; then LPT secondary rules on player-card technical standards, affordability-check thresholds and the 2027–28 phasing.
LPT's FY26 release (expected Feb–Mar 2027): whether Q4-26 confirms the Q3 slowdown (derived +9%) and whether remote betting recovers without a major tournament.
Confirmation that the 1 Jan 2028 complete advertising ban is on the statute book and how LPT polices foreign-brand advertising after its Feb 2026 exchange with the industry association.
Enforcement consistency on prediction markets (Kalshi) and the size of the blacklist; any LPT or Ministry estimate of the illegal market and tax leakage.
Retail indicators — machine count (3,736 at Sep-26), venue closures and licence surrenders — as the leading signal for consolidation opportunities ahead of 2029 cashless capex.
Status of the reported €1,000 per-month loss-limit proposal and of lottery-licence policy (two operators), both of which would reshape the wallet split.

Tax rates/bases are from the State Tax Inspectorate (VMI) and corroborated by actual collections (gambling tax 21.8% of GGR; lottery tax 18.4% of sales). FX: EUR/USD ~1.094, as implied by press conversions on 23–24 Nov 2026 (€229m = $250.5m); not verified against the ECB reference rate — all ~USD figures are approximate. Unverified/flagged: one-off licence fee (~€1m, press-implied); SBC-cited venue counts (18 casinos/50 halls/10 online licences); pre-July-2022 tax rates; the name of the second lottery operator; operator brand list and shares; status of the €1,000/month limit; whether the 2028 advertising ban is already enacted (secondary sources only); Gaming Intelligence Q1/Q2 figures assumed to include lottery GGR; Q3-26 and 9M-25 product figures are derived by subtraction; FY26E/FY27E are analyst estimates.
